messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Evan was 28, a European American man working as a social media manager, and when he first described the event that brought him to treatment he did so in a careful, rehearsed way, as if he had learned to keep the account tidy because the real thing felt too large and too strange to say plainly. The trauma had occurred during military service, in a situation that he still found difficult to make fully real even now. He could remember it in disconnected pieces: the sound of a helicopter passing overhead, the sharp sight of injuries on other people, his own body jolting into action, and then stretches that were harder to place in sequence. When he tried to tell it straight through, the story seemed to break apart in his mouth. He would pause, look down, and say that part of what unsettled him was that he could sometimes feel all of the fear, dread, and helplessness again without being able to call up a clear image of what had happened. The event lived in him as fragments and as a kind of emotional blast, and that mismatch made him feel as though the memory itself was almost unbelievable, something that should belong to someone else rather than to him.

In the months after returning home, Evan began organizing his life around the situations that set that experience off. He avoided military and police uniforms and weapons wherever he could, taking different routes when he saw someone in uniform and turning away from news clips or public spaces where firearms were visible. In his job, where he managed online content, he became vigilant about the material he might encounter on screens and would sometimes ask a colleague to handle posts that included images of wounds or injuries, because seeing visible injuries on others could jolt him back into the same state of alarm he had felt during service. He also found himself shrinking from ordinary social situations that involved driving with other people. If a friend offered him a ride or his partner suggested they go somewhere together, he would often insist on taking separate cars or finding another way, not because he disliked the company but because being in a car with someone else made him feel trapped in a way he could not easily explain. Over time he also began rehearsing what he would say before almost any interaction, whether it was a meeting at work, ordering coffee, or speaking with his partner’s family. He would run through sentences in advance, worried that if he was caught off guard he might say the wrong thing or appear visibly shaken. He started avoiding situations that would put his body under stress as well, declining hikes, gym sessions, and anything physically demanding, because heightened bodily strain made him feel too close to the raw panic he associated with the traumatic period.

At night, Evan’s efforts to stay alert did not stop once he got into bed. He would lie there listening, unable to settle quickly because some part of him remained on guard, as though sleep were a time when something could happen without warning. His partner had noticed that he took longer to fall asleep and often asked if he was okay when he remained rigid and watchful in the dark. He was also startled when touched unexpectedly, especially if someone came up behind him or brushed his arm without warning. He would flinch hard enough to embarrass himself, his heart racing before he had time to recognize who had touched him. Certain sounds could do it too: the distant thrum of a helicopter or aircraft made his stomach drop and his body react before he had processed where he was. He said that the reactions felt immediate and physical, as if his body had not received the message that the danger was over, even while another part of him knew he was sitting in a safe apartment or walking down an ordinary city street.

As these changes accumulated, Evan became more convinced that he had been altered in a way that set him apart from other people. He told the therapist that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and he spoke about it with a mix of shame and disbelief, as though his presence in the event revealed something fundamentally different about him. He had come to believe that he was permanently an outsider now, even among people who cared about him. That sense of distance made ordinary closeness harder; he could be affectionate with his partner and still feel, in the next moment, that there was a private zone of experience no one else could enter. The relationship remained important to him, but the gap between what he felt internally and what he could say aloud widened over time.

He eventually sought help because the combination of his sleep problems, his startle reactions, and the growing restrictions on his everyday life were becoming harder to manage. Work demanded that he stay composed and responsive, yet he found himself spending extra time preparing for conversations and avoiding content that might contain injuries or weapons. Social plans were becoming more complicated because he was reluctant to drive with others or do anything that left him physically keyed up. At intake, what he most wanted was to feel less as though he had been permanently changed for the worse, and what he most feared was that the strange, fragmented memory and the sudden waves of fear would keep arriving without warning, leaving him trapped in a body that still seemed to be waiting for the next helicopter, the next touch, the next flash of injury.
